title: Ha Mim: two letters that ask you to pay attention.
subtitle: A pause before the surah begins
then: This surah was revealed in Makkah while the leaders of Quraysh were plotting against the Prophet ﷺ. It opens with two letters, Ha and Mim. {idea}Their meaning is known to Allah.{/idea} What follows is an oath by the clear Book.
now: You open the app between messages, half reading, half thinking about dinner. Two letters you cannot explain sit at the top of the page. {idea}Let them be a doorbell.{/idea} Something is about to be said to you.
old: Letters I do not understand are something to rush past.
new: Not knowing their meaning, I can still let them wake me up to listen.
try: Before reading the next surah you open, take one slow breath and put the phone on silent.

title: Sworn by the Book that is clear.
subtitle: Why Allah swears by the clear Book
then: Ibn Kathir explains the Book is called clear because it is {idea}plain in both wording and meaning{/idea}. It came in the Arabic of the people who first heard it, so they could not say they did not understand.
now: You tell yourself you will read the Quran properly once you have time to study. So you never start. {idea}It calls itself clear.{/idea} A translation and ten quiet minutes is enough to begin.
old: The Quran is too complicated for someone like me.
new: It was sent clear on purpose, so I can understand it.
try: Read the translation of one short passage today and write one sentence on what it says.

title: Sent in a language they knew, so they would think.
subtitle: The Quran is meant to be understood and pondered
then: The first listeners were Arabs, people who loved eloquent speech. Ibn Kathir says the Quran was sent in their language {idea}so that you may understand it and ponder its meanings{/idea}.
now: In Ramadan you race to finish the whole Quran, eyes moving faster than understanding. You close it proud and remember nothing. {idea}The verse gives the goal: to understand.{/idea}
old: What counts is how much I read.
new: What counts is that the words reach my mind and heart.
try: Read just three verses today, then close your eyes and ask what they mean for you.

title: Honored with Allah before it ever reached you.
subtitle: The Quran's high place in the Mother of the Book
then: Ibn Kathir says the Mother of the Book is {idea}the Preserved Tablet{/idea}, as Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said. The verse shows the Quran's high status among those on high, {reward}so that people on earth will respect it and follow it{/reward}.
now: Your copy of the Quran sits under a stack of mail and a phone charger. Nobody meant disrespect. {idea}But this book is honored in a place far above us.{/idea}
old: The Quran is a book like any other on my shelf.
new: It holds a place of honor with Allah, and I can give it that place in my home.
try: Give your Quran a clean, high, uncluttered spot today.

title: They turned away, and the reminder kept coming.
subtitle: Mercy that does not give up on people
then: The question is: should We stop the reminder because you went too far? Qatadah said that if the Quran had been taken away when the first generation rejected it, they would have been doomed, {reward}but Allah by His mercy kept sending it and calling them{/reward}.
now: You have ignored the same reminder for years: the Friday talk, the friend's gentle text, the verse that keeps showing up. And still it keeps coming. {reward}That is not an accident. That is mercy.{/reward}
old: I have ignored it so long, Allah must be done with me.
new: The reminder still reaching me is proof He has not given up on me.
try: Notice one reminder that keeps returning in your life. Answer it with one small step today.

title: You are not the first to be sent.
subtitle: Comfort for the Prophet: many came before
then: Ibn Kathir says here Allah {idea}consoles His Prophet ﷺ for the disbelief of his people{/idea} and tells him to be patient. Many prophets had been sent to earlier communities.
now: You are the only one in your office who prays, or the first in your family to take faith seriously. It can feel lonely. {idea}You stand in a long line of people who were in the same place.{/idea}
old: I am alone in trying to do the right thing.
new: Many before me walked this road, and Allah comforted them on it.
try: Read about one prophet's story this week and notice what he faced from his people.

title: Every prophet was mocked. Mockery proves nothing.
subtitle: Ridicule is the old reply to truth
then: Ibn Kathir explains that no prophet came to those people except that {trap}they disbelieved him and mocked him{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ in Makkah faced the same thing, so he was not to be shaken by it.
now: You mention in the group chat that you will not join because of prayer time. A laughing emoji, a "here we go." Your face gets warm. {idea}Being laughed at does not make you wrong.{/idea}
old: If people laugh at what I believe, maybe I should hide it.
new: Mockery has met every prophet. It says nothing about the truth.
try: Next time a small joke comes at your faith, smile, stay kind, and do not change course.

title: Stronger people fell before. Their story is a lesson.
subtitle: Power did not protect those who mocked
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah destroyed those who rejected the messengers, and {trap}they were stronger in power{/trap} than the Quraysh. Others said the example of the ancients means {idea}their lesson{/idea} for those who came after.
now: You feel untouchable at your peak: good job, good health, a full bank account. That is when it is easiest to ignore advice. {idea}History is full of strong people who thought the same.{/idea}
old: As long as I am strong, I do not need to change.
new: Strength has never protected anyone from the results of their choices.
try: Think of one warning you brushed off because things were going well. Take it seriously today.

title: They knew who created everything, then served others.
subtitle: Admitting the Creator but not living by it
then: Ibn Kathir says the idolaters of Makkah {idea}admitted that Allah alone created everything{/idea}, {trap}yet they still worshipped idols and false gods alongside Him{/trap}.
now: Ask yourself who provides your income and you will say Allah. Then watch where your worry goes at 3am: the boss's mood, the market, the landlord. {trap}The answer and the anxiety point in different directions.{/trap}
old: Saying Allah is the Creator is the same as trusting Him.
new: Believing He made everything should change where I turn when I am afraid.
try: When you next feel worry about money, say "Allah created this and me" before you open the banking app.

title: A steady earth and roads to find your way.
subtitle: The ground under you is a gift
then: Ibn Kathir explains the earth was made {reward}smooth, stable and firm{/reward} so people can walk, stand and sleep on it, held firm by mountains. Paths run between mountains and valleys so travelers {idea}find their way{/idea} from land to land.
now: You drive to work on autopilot, map app open, never once thinking about the ground staying still under the car. {reward}A steady earth is something given, every morning.{/reward}
old: The ground and the roads are just there.
new: The steady earth and the paths across it are prepared for me, so I can find my way.
try: On your next walk or drive, notice the ground once and say alhamdulillah for it.

title: Rain revives dead land. So will you be raised.
subtitle: The measured rain and the coming resurrection
then: Ibn Kathir says the rain comes {reward}in due measure{/reward}, enough for crops and drinking. When it reaches barren land, it stirs to life, and in this Allah {idea}draws attention to how He will bring bodies back to life{/idea} on the Day of Resurrection.
now: A dry patch of lawn after weeks of heat. One night of rain and by the weekend it is green. You notice and think nothing of it. {idea}It is a small preview of your own rising.{/idea}
old: Rain and new growth are just nature doing its thing.
new: Every revived field is a reminder that I will be brought back too.
try: Next time it rains, step outside for one minute and remember the Day you will rise.

title: Pairs of everything, and the rides that carry you.
subtitle: Creation in pairs, ships and animals made easy
then: Ibn Kathir explains the pairs are of {idea}everything that grows, and all kinds of animals{/idea}. He made ships and cattle {reward}easy for people to use{/reward}: to eat their meat, drink their milk, and ride on their backs.
now: Your morning: a train, a bus, a car, maybe a flight next week. Milk in your coffee. You did not invent any of it, and you rarely think who made it possible. {reward}Everything that carries you was made to be carried on.{/reward}
old: Transport and food are just how life works now.
new: Every ride and every meal is something He made easy for me.
try: Before your next commute, pause and think of one thing that carries you that you never thank Him for.

title: When you sit on your ride, remember who made it yours.
subtitle: The words to say when you set off

row.title: you settle in
sub: on the back, in the seat

then: The verse teaches words to say when mounting. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and others explained: {idea}we could not have done this ourselves{/idea}. If Allah had not made these animals obedient, no human strength could have.
now: You get in the car, seatbelt on, phone into the holder, music on. Two tons of metal at high speed, and you feel fully in charge. {idea}This verse gives you one sentence to say before you pull out.{/idea}
old: I am in control of my car and my journey.
new: I travel only because He made it possible. I could not do it alone.
try: Say "Glory to Him who has subjected this to us" the next time you start a journey.

title: Every trip points to the final one home.
subtitle: To our Lord we will return
then: Ibn Kathir notes that {idea}mention of earthly journeys draws attention to the journey of the Hereafter{/idea}. He links it to the verse that says take provision, but {reward}the best provision is taqwa{/reward}.
now: At the airport you check three times: passport, charger, boarding pass. Everything for a two-week trip. {idea}This verse asks what you are packing for the journey that has no return ticket.{/idea}
old: Travel is just about getting where I am going.
new: Every departure reminds me I am heading back to my Lord.
try: On your next trip, make one good deed part of the packing: a charity, a call, a prayer.

title: They gave His servants a share in Him.
subtitle: Turning creatures into partners of the Creator

row.title: credit shared out
sub: a bit for Him, a bit for others

then: Ibn Kathir links this to the Makkan practice of {trap}setting aside some of their crops and cattle for Allah and some for their idols{/trap}. In the same way they assigned Him a share from among His own servants. The verse calls this plain ingratitude.
now: You get the job and thank your contacts, your CV, your luck, your interview coach. Allah gets a quick mention at the end, if at all. {trap}The credit is split among creatures.{/trap}
old: Thanking Allah once, alongside everyone else, is enough.
new: Everything good came from Him, so the deepest thanks belongs to Him alone.
try: For one blessing this week, thank Allah first and fully before you thank anyone else.

title: Daughters for Him, sons for you? An unfair split.
subtitle: Giving Allah what you yourself rejected
then: The Quraysh claimed the angels were daughters of Allah, while they prized sons for themselves. Ibn Kathir calls this {trap}a denunciation in the strongest terms{/trap} and links it to the verse: is it for you the males and for Him the females? {trap}That is a division most unfair.{/trap}
now: You give the best hours of your day to work and scrolling, and the tired leftover minutes to prayer. The prime cut for you, the scraps for Him. {idea}Look at what you set aside for Allah.{/idea}
old: Allah gets whatever I have left over.
new: Giving Allah what I would not accept for myself is the same unfair split.
try: Give Allah one of your best moments tomorrow: pray Fajr before checking your phone.

title: His face darkened at news of a baby girl.
subtitle: The double standard exposed

key.label: What news of a daughter is

then: Ibn Kathir explains that when one of them heard a daughter was born, {trap}he hated the news and kept away from people out of shame{/trap}. Allah asks: how can they dislike something so much for themselves, and then attribute it to Him? Note the verse calls the birth {reward}good tidings{/reward}.
now: The ultrasound says girl, and a relative sighs on the phone. Or a father, quietly, wishes it were different. {reward}The Quran called that news good tidings{/reward}, and shows the dark face as the problem.
old: Some news about a child is a disappointment.
new: The birth of a daughter is good news, and the frown is what is wrong.
try: Congratulate a family with a newborn daughter warmly and specifically this week, or pray for one.

title: Their own view of girls undid their own claim.
subtitle: Arguing against them with their own logic
then: The verse argues with the Quraysh using {idea}their own standards{/idea}. Ibn Kathir describes how they viewed girls as lacking, raised in ornaments and unable to argue in a dispute, {trap}and yet they attributed daughters to Allah{/trap}. By their own logic their claim collapses.
now: You catch yourself treating people one way when it suits you and the opposite way when it does not. A rule for your team, another for theirs. {trap}The verse shows that kind of double standard falling apart on its own.{/trap}
old: My standards are consistent and fair.
new: When my beliefs contradict my own standards, something is wrong with the belief.
try: Pick one strong opinion you hold. Ask: would I accept the same rule if it applied to me?

title: Were you there when they were created?
subtitle: Claims about the unseen will be questioned
then: The Quraysh said the angels were female. Allah asks: {idea}did they witness their creation?{/idea} Ibn Kathir says their testimony {trap}will be recorded and they will be questioned{/trap} about it on the Day of Resurrection, a stern warning.
now: Someone forwards a message: "this angel visits you if you share this." You hit forward without thinking. {trap}Everything said about Allah and the unseen is written down.{/trap}
old: It does not hurt to repeat religious claims I have heard.
new: Anything I say about Allah or the unseen will be recorded and asked about.
try: Before forwarding any religious message today, check the source or do not send it.

title: If Allah did not want it, I would not do it.
subtitle: Using His decree as an excuse
then: Ibn Kathir explains they said: if Allah had willed, He would have stopped us, so {trap}He must approve{/trap}. They used Allah's decree as an excuse, and he notes this reasoning only showed their ignorance. Every messenger brought the same command: worship Him alone.
now: "If it was not meant to be, it would not have happened." You say it after skipping a prayer, after a harsh word, after a habit you know is wrong. {trap}Destiny becomes the excuse.{/trap}
old: If Allah did not want me to do this, He would stop me.
new: His decree is never my excuse. I know what He asked, and I choose.
try: Catch one moment today when you say "it was meant to be" about your own mistake. Own it instead.

title: Where is your book for this?
subtitle: Beliefs with no source behind them
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah condemns them for {trap}worshipping others with no evidence or proof{/trap}. Did We give them a book before this to hold onto? He answers: that did not happen.
now: Some things you do because "that is how it is done": a ritual at weddings, a superstition about the evil eye, a rule you were told as a kid. Ask the simple question. {idea}Where does this come from?{/idea}
old: If it is part of my religion, it must have a source.
new: Every belief I hold should be able to answer: where is the proof?
try: Pick one religious habit you never questioned and look up where it actually comes from.

title: We found our fathers doing it. That was all.
subtitle: Tradition as the only argument
then: Ibn Kathir says they had {trap}no grounds for their belief apart from imitating their fathers and forefathers{/trap}. Their claim to be guided by those footsteps came with no evidence.
now: "In our family we have always done it this way." Said about money, about anger, about how a wife or husband is treated, about grudges against relatives. {idea}Family habit is not the same as guidance.{/idea}
old: If my parents did it, it must be right.
new: I can love my family and still ask if their way matches the truth.
try: Name one family habit you copied without thinking. Ask if it is guidance or just habit.

title: The comfortable always said the same thing.
subtitle: Why the affluent clung to the old way
then: The verse names {trap}the affluent{/trap} of every town as the ones who answered warners this way. Ibn Kathir notes these people said the same thing nation after nation: {trap}their hearts and their words are similar{/trap}.
now: When life is comfortable, any call to change feels like a threat. The good salary, the easy routine. It is easy to say "this is how I have always lived." {idea}Comfort can be the loudest voice against truth.{/idea}
old: I resist this change because of my values.
new: Sometimes I resist change because my comfort is at stake.
try: Think of one change you keep resisting. Ask honestly: is it principle, or comfort?

title: Even if I bring you something better?
subtitle: When better guidance is still refused
then: Each warner asked: even if I bring you better guidance than your fathers had? Ibn Kathir says even if they were convinced, {trap}they would not follow it, because of their evil intentions and arrogance{/trap} toward the truth and its people.
now: A friend shows you, kindly, a better way to handle money or an argument. It is clearly better. And still you say no, because accepting it means admitting you were wrong. {trap}Pride shuts the door, not the evidence.{/trap}
old: I would change if someone showed me something better.
new: Sometimes I have already been shown something better, and pride is what keeps me from it.
try: Accept one piece of good advice this week that you resisted only because of who said it.

title: See how the deniers ended.
subtitle: The end of stubborn rejection
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah took retribution on the disbelieving nations with {trap}various kinds of punishment{/trap}, as told in their stories. The command is to look: {idea}see what became of them, and how Allah saved the believers{/idea}.
now: You hear the stories of earlier nations at Friday prayer and file them under history. The verse says "see," as in look closely, and learn. {idea}The point is your own choices, not theirs.{/idea}
old: Stories of destroyed nations are about other people long ago.
new: Their end is shown to me so I can choose differently today.
try: Read one story of a past nation in the Quran and write down one lesson for yourself.

title: Ibrahim broke with his father's way, out loud.
subtitle: The ancestor they claimed did not follow tradition
then: The Quraysh said they followed their fathers. Ibn Kathir reminds that Ibrahim was {idea}the leader of the monotheists, from whom Quraysh were descended{/idea} and claimed their religion. And he {idea}disowned his father's and his people's idol worship{/idea}.
now: You are the first in your family to stop a certain habit: the lottery tickets, the fortune teller, the drinking at weddings. It feels like betraying them. {idea}Ibrahim did exactly this, gently and clearly.{/idea}
old: Breaking from my family's way is disloyal.
new: Loyalty to the truth can mean stepping away from what my family does, as Ibrahim did.
try: Name one inherited habit you know is wrong. Decide on one kind sentence to explain why you stopped.

title: Except the One who made me. He will guide me.
subtitle: Leaving the false with trust in the true
then: Ibrahim did not leave a void. He rejected the idols {idea}except Him Who created me{/idea}, and declared he trusted Allah to guide him. Ibn Kathir calls this his {idea}declaration of tawhid{/idea}.
now: You quit the job that made you compromise. Or you leave a friend group that pulled you the wrong way. The next morning the space feels empty. {reward}Ibrahim's words fill it: He will guide me.{/reward}
old: If I leave what I know, I will be lost.
new: The One who created me will show me the next step.
try: Say "He will guide me" before one uncertain decision today.

title: He left one word behind for his children.
subtitle: La ilaha illallah as a family inheritance
then: Ibn Kathir says the word means {reward}La ilaha illallah{/reward}: worship of Allah alone. Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah and others said there are still those among his offspring who say it. He left it {idea}so that they may come back to it{/idea}.
now: You think about what you will leave your kids: a house, savings, maybe a business. Ibrahim left a sentence, and people are still saying it thousands of years later. {reward}What word will your children inherit from you?{/reward}
old: The best thing I can leave my children is security.
new: The best inheritance is a word of faith they can always come back to.
try: Tonight, say La ilaha illallah aloud near your children or family, and tell them what it means to you.

title: A long, easy life, until the truth arrived.
subtitle: Enjoyment was a delay, not approval

row.title: life is easy, so I am fine

then: Ibn Kathir explains the idolaters and their fathers {trap}lived a long life in their misguidance{/trap}. Then came the truth with a Messenger ﷺ whose {idea}message and warning were clear{/idea}.
now: Years of comfort: decent job, healthy kids, no crisis. Faith sits in the background. Then one day a clear reminder lands in front of you, a talk, a death, a verse. {idea}The easy years were time given, not a sign that nothing needs to change.{/idea}
old: My life is going well, so I must be on the right path.
new: Ease is time to prepare, and the truth asks for an answer when it arrives.
try: Think of the clearest reminder you received this year. Respond to it with one action today.

title: When truth came, they called it magic.
subtitle: Labelling the truth to avoid facing it
then: Ibn Kathir says when the truth came they were {trap}arrogant and stubborn, and pushed him away out of disbelief, envy and transgression{/trap}. Calling it magic was their way of dismissing it.
now: A sharp truth about you lands in an argument, and you reply "you are just being dramatic." A label, and the conversation is over. {trap}Naming something to dismiss it is the oldest trick.{/trap}
old: If I can label it, I do not need to deal with it.
new: Calling the truth a name does not make it go away. It only shows I am avoiding it.
try: Next time you want to dismiss a criticism with a label, pause and ask if part of it is true.

title: Why not a big man from the two cities?
subtitle: Judging the message by the status of the messenger
then: The Quraysh asked why the Quran was not sent to a prominent man from {trap}Makkah or At-Taif{/trap}, as Ibn Abbas and others explained. Some scholars said they meant Al-Walid bin Al-Mughirah and Urwah bin Masud. Their measure was status.
now: A young imam gives a talk and you tune out, waiting for the famous speaker. A junior colleague has the right idea and nobody listens until the manager repeats it. {trap}We judge the message by the size of the name.{/trap}
old: I listen more to people who are important.
new: Truth can come through anyone Allah chooses, rank has nothing to do with it.
try: This week, listen fully to someone you usually overlook, and take one thing they say seriously.

title: Do they hand out your Lord's mercy?
subtitle: Different ranks, shared need, and a better mercy
then: Allah answers: {idea}is it they who would portion out the mercy of your Lord?{/idea} Ibn Kathir says He divides wealth, intellect and strength among people so that {idea}one needs the other{/idea}. And {reward}His mercy is better than the wealth they gather{/reward}.
now: Payday. You compare salaries in your head: the friend who earns double, the cousin with the bigger house. You feel small. {reward}The verse says the thing worth wanting is not on the payslip.{/reward}
old: Someone who earns more than me is worth more.
new: Rank is a way for people to need each other. His mercy is the real wealth.
try: Thank one person whose work you depend on but rarely notice: a cleaner, a driver, a cashier.

title: Silver roofs would mean nothing to Allah.
subtitle: Wealth is not a sign of His love
then: Ibn Abbas, Al-Hasan and others explained: if not for the risk that ignorant people would think {trap}wealth was a sign that Allah loves its owner{/trap}, and all choose disbelief for it, He would have given disbelievers {trap}roofs and stairways of silver{/trap}.
now: You see a wealthy influencer living carelessly and think, maybe this is what success with God looks like. {idea}The verse says if wealth were a reward for goodness, Allah would not hand it out so freely.{/idea}
old: Rich people must be doing something right with God.
new: Wealth is so small to Allah that He gives it even to those who reject Him.
try: Next time you envy someone's lifestyle online, say "this is the enjoyment of this world" and close the app.

title: Silver doors, silver couches, and still nothing.
subtitle: Luxury that weighs nothing with Allah
then: Ibn Kathir explains the doors and couches would all be of silver too. He cites a hadith narrated by Al-Baghawi: {idea}if this world were worth a gnat's wing before Allah{/idea}, He would not give a disbeliever a drink of water.
now: You scroll through home tours: marble floors, a sofa that costs a year's rent. You start a savings plan for things you do not need. {idea}The verse adds up all that luxury and calls it small.{/idea}
old: The dream home would finally make me happy.
new: Even a palace of silver is almost nothing in Allah's sight.
try: Unfollow one account that makes you want luxury you do not need.

title: Gold is brief. The Hereafter is for the mindful.
subtitle: What is kept for those with taqwa
then: Ibn Kathir tells how Umar found the Prophet ﷺ resting on {trap}a rough mat that had left marks on his side{/trap} and wept, comparing him to Caesar and Chosroes. The Prophet ﷺ sat up and said those were people whose good things were hastened for them in this life. {reward}The Hereafter is for the mindful.{/reward}
now: You visit a friend with a huge house and come home to your small flat feeling poor. The sofa is old, the paint is peeling. {reward}Umar wept over a rough mat, and the answer was: the Hereafter is better.{/reward}
old: Others have more, so they are better off than me.
new: Gold here ends. What is with my Lord lasts for those who are mindful of Him.
try: Look around your home and thank Allah for three simple things you have, out loud.

title: Turn away from His remembrance, and a devil moves in.
subtitle: Blindness of the heart invites a bad companion
then: Ibn Kathir explains the word used comes from {trap}weakness of vision{/trap}, meaning here weakness of insight: willfully ignoring the remembrance of the Most Gracious. For that person {trap}a devil is assigned as a companion{/trap}.
now: You drop your morning adhkar for a few weeks. Not on purpose, just busy. Slowly the mornings fill with doomscrolling, irritation, a heavier mood. {trap}A heart does not stay empty.{/trap}
old: Skipping remembrance just leaves a blank space.
new: When I stop remembering Allah, something worse takes that space.
try: Bring back one small remembrance tomorrow morning: three times subhanallah before you get out of bed.

title: Pulled off the path, while sure they are guided.
subtitle: The danger of feeling right while going wrong

row.title: I feel fine, so I am fine

then: Ibn Kathir says for the one who willfully neglects guidance, {trap}a devil is sent to lead him astray and show him the path to Hell{/trap}. The frightening part is in the verse: {trap}they think they are guided{/trap}.
now: You feel completely sure in an argument, sure about a habit, sure about a grudge. Everyone around you is wrong. {idea}Feeling certain is not the same as being on the path.{/idea}
old: If I feel at peace with it, it must be right.
new: I can feel guided and still be drifting, so I check myself against revelation.
try: Ask one trusted, honest person: "Is there something I am doing that I cannot see is wrong?"

title: I wish you were as far from me as east from west.
subtitle: Regretting a companion on the Day
then: Ibn Kathir says when he comes before Allah on the Day of Resurrection, {trap}he will complain about the devil who was assigned to him{/trap}. He wishes the distance between them were as far as the east from the west.
now: The friend who always says "one more round," the online voice who makes everything cynical. You enjoy it now. {idea}Picture that friendship from the end, and ask if you will still want them close.{/idea}
old: My friends do not really affect who I become.
new: The companions I keep close now are the ones I will be judged alongside.
try: Spend time this week with one friend who reminds you of Allah.

title: Sharing the blame will not lighten it.
subtitle: Company in wrongdoing is no comfort later
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}your being together in the Fire will not help you in the slightest{/trap}, and both will share in the painful punishment. Having company in wrongdoing changes nothing.
now: At work, everyone pads their expense report a little. In the family, everyone gossips about the same aunt. It feels safer because it is shared. {idea}The verse says sharing it does not shrink your part.{/idea}
old: If everyone is doing it, it is not that bad.
new: A wrong shared with others is still fully mine.
try: Step out of one shared wrong this week, quietly, even if you are the only one.

title: You cannot make the deaf hear. That is not your job.
subtitle: Guidance belongs to Allah, the message to you
then: Ibn Kathir says this means {idea}that is not up to you{/idea}. The Prophet ﷺ only had to convey the message, and {idea}Allah guides whom He wills{/idea}, being Wise and Just in that.
now: Your brother has stopped praying. You have tried talks, texts, videos, guilt. You lie awake feeling responsible. {idea}Your part is to be kind and clear. The heart is in Allah's hands.{/idea}
old: If someone I love does not change, it is my failure.
new: I deliver with love. Opening hearts is Allah's work, not mine.
try: Make dua for one person you have been trying to change, then let go of the pressure for today.

title: Even after you are gone, justice will come.
subtitle: The outcome does not depend on the Prophet's lifetime

row.title: it will happen
sub: whether I see it or not

then: The surah introduction notes the Makkan leaders were {trap}plotting day and night to end the Prophet's ﷺ life{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says the verse means {idea}We will inevitably punish them, even if you pass away{/idea}.
now: Someone wronged your family badly and seems to be doing fine. You worry you will die before anything is set right. {idea}The verse says the account stays open, whether or not you are there to see it close.{/idea}
old: If I do not see justice myself, it never happened.
new: Allah's justice does not wait on my lifetime.
try: Hand one old injustice over to Allah in a dua, and let yourself rest from carrying it.

title: Or We will show you. We are able to do both.
subtitle: Allah's full control over the outcome
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah is able to do both. As-Suddi's view, favored by Ibn Jarir, is that {reward}Allah would not take His Messenger ﷺ until He let him see his enemies brought low{/reward} and gave him power over them.
now: You are up against something huge: a company, a system, an illness. It feels unbeatable. {idea}Nothing is beyond His command.{/idea} How and when it turns is His to decide.
old: Some things are just too big to change.
new: Whatever I face is under the full command of Allah.
try: Write down the problem that feels too big. Under it write: "He has full command over this."

title: Hold tight to what was revealed. You are on the path.
subtitle: Steadiness under pressure
then: With plots all around him, the Prophet ﷺ is told to hold fast. Ibn Kathir says this means {idea}hold fast to the Quran which has been sent down to your heart{/idea}, for it is truth and leads to {reward}the straight path to the Gardens{/reward}.
now: Everyone around you is cutting corners and you start wondering if you are naive. The pressure is real. {idea}The verse does not say "relax." It says "hold tighter."{/idea}
old: When everyone pushes back, maybe I should loosen up.
new: Pressure is exactly when I hold on tighter to what Allah sent.
try: When you feel pressure to compromise today, recite one verse you know by heart before you decide.

title: An honor for you, and you will be asked about it.
subtitle: The Quran as both privilege and responsibility

picture.label: What it means to have it

row.title: a question
sub: what did you do with it

then: Ibn Abbas and others said this means {reward}an honor for you and your people{/reward}, revealed in their language, so they were most obliged to follow it. Ibn Kathir adds: {idea}you will be questioned about how you acted on it{/idea}.
now: Three copies of the Quran in your house, an app on your phone, a beautiful recitation in your car. It is easier to reach than ever. {idea}And one day the question: what did you do with it?{/idea}
old: Having the Quran in my life is the honor.
new: The honor comes with a question: how did I respond to it?
try: Choose one verse and act on it today in one concrete way.

title: Ask every messenger. They all said the same.
subtitle: One message across all prophets
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}all the messengers called their people to the same{/idea}: worship Allah alone, and leave idols and false gods. The Prophet ﷺ was bringing nothing new.
now: A friend tells you Islam is just one opinion among many. You realize you have never thought of it as the same message Ibrahim, Musa and Isa brought. {idea}One call, from the first messenger to the last.{/idea}
old: My faith is one tradition among many separate ones.
new: Every messenger called to the same thing: worship the Merciful alone.
try: Read the story of one other prophet this week and notice the same core message.

title: Musa walked into Pharaoh's court with one sentence.
subtitle: I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds
then: Ibn Kathir says Musa was sent to Pharaoh and {trap}his governors, ministers and leaders{/trap}, to call them to {idea}worship Allah alone{/idea}. He came with mighty signs like his hand and his staff. The story is told to the Quraysh, who faced the same message.
now: A meeting where the most powerful person in the room says something you know is wrong. Everyone nods. {idea}Musa's whole speech was one clear sentence.{/idea} Sometimes that is all it takes.
old: Before powerful people, it is safer to say nothing.
new: Truth can be said simply and calmly, even in front of power.
try: In one conversation this week, say one true thing clearly that you would normally swallow.

title: Clear signs, and at once they laughed.
subtitle: Laughter as a shield against the truth
then: Ibn Kathir says despite the signs they {trap}remained arrogant and stubbornly refused to follow him{/trap}. They made fun of the message and {trap}laughed at the one who had brought it{/trap}.
now: A serious reminder comes up at the dinner table and someone makes a joke, and everyone laughs, and the moment is gone. Maybe you made the joke. {idea}Laughter can be a way to avoid thinking.{/idea}
old: Joking about serious things is harmless.
new: Sometimes I laugh at a truth because I do not want to face it.
try: Next time a reminder makes you uncomfortable, resist the joke and sit with it for a moment.

title: Each sign bigger than the last, so they might return.
subtitle: Hardship as a call to come back
then: Ibn Kathir lists the signs: {trap}the flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood{/trap}, and loss of crops and lives. Each was greater than the one before, yet they would not give up their sin. The verse states the aim: {reward}that perhaps they might return{/reward}.
now: A health scare, then a job loss, then a car breakdown. It feels like the universe is against you. {reward}The verse frames hardship as an invitation back, not only a blow.{/reward}
old: A run of bad things means life is unfair.
new: Hardship can be Allah calling me back to Him.
try: In your current difficulty, ask: "What might Allah be calling me back to?" Write one answer.

title: Please pray for us. We promise we will change.
subtitle: Promises made only in desperation
then: Every time a sign hit, they came to Musa calling him "sorcerer," which Ibn Jarir explains meant {idea}knowledgeable one{/idea} in their time, a title of respect. {trap}They promised to believe and to free the Children of Israel{/trap} if the torment was lifted.
now: In the hospital corridor waiting for news, you make promises: I will pray every prayer, I will call my father, I will stop. It is sincere in that moment. {trap}The test is what happens when the doctor says it is fine.{/trap}
old: The promises I make in a crisis show who I really am.
new: Who I really am shows after the crisis passes.
try: Remember one promise you made to Allah in a hard moment. Keep one part of it today.

title: The torment lifted, and the promise vanished.
subtitle: Breaking your word once relief comes
then: Ibn Kathir notes that {trap}on each occasion they went back on their word{/trap}. The cycle repeated: affliction, a promise, relief, then broken word.
now: The scan came back clear. Two weeks later, the promises have faded and life is the same as before. You barely remember how scared you were. {trap}At once, the verse says. That fast.{/trap}
old: Once things are fine, I can go back to normal.
new: Relief is not the end of the deal. It is when keeping my word counts.
try: Write down the last thing Allah relieved you from and one promise you will keep because of it.

title: Is Egypt not mine? Look at my rivers.
subtitle: Pharaoh's proof was his property

row.title: the truth itself
sub: not the size of the estate

then: Ibn Kathir says Pharaoh assembled his people and spoke {trap}in a vainglorious fashion, boasting of his dominion{/trap}. Qatadah said they had gardens and flowing rivers. "Do you not see?" meant: see my might, and how poor and weak Musa's followers are.
now: In an argument, you pull rank: "I have been in this job twenty years." "I pay the bills in this house." {trap}What you own becomes your argument.{/trap}
old: My position and possessions prove I know best.
new: Owning more does not make me right. Only the truth does.
try: In your next disagreement, argue from the point itself, not from your position or what you have.

title: Mocking the messenger to dodge the message.
subtitle: Pharaoh attacks Musa's speech and status
then: Pharaoh called Musa {trap}despicable{/trap}, meaning, as Ibn Jarir said, without power, authority or wealth, and said he could not speak clearly. Ibn Kathir calls this a lie: Musa had prayed and Allah answered, and {idea}a person cannot be blamed for physical matters beyond his control{/idea}.
now: In a meeting, someone shoots down a good idea by mocking the accent or stammer of the person who said it. Everyone laughs. {trap}The idea never even gets discussed.{/trap}
old: How someone speaks tells me how much they are worth listening to.
new: Attacking how someone looks or talks is a way to avoid what they said.
try: Next time you hear someone mocked for how they speak, steer the room back to their point.

title: Where are his gold bracelets? Where are his angels?
subtitle: Judging by outward show
then: Ibn Kathir says golden bracelets were adornments of rank, as Ibn Abbas and Qatadah explained. Pharaoh {trap}looked only at outward appearances{/trap} and did not understand {idea}the inner matters that are clearer{/idea}.
now: You judge a guest by their car, a teacher by their clothes, a speaker by how many followers they have. {trap}The entourage impresses you.{/trap} The substance goes unnoticed.
old: Status symbols tell me who matters.
new: What matters is often hidden behind a plain appearance.
try: Today, notice one person you judged by looks and find out one thing about their character.

title: He made his people light-minded, and they obeyed.
subtitle: Being led because you let yourself be fooled
then: Ibn Kathir explains Pharaoh {trap}confused them and invited them to misguidance, and they responded{/trap}. The verse adds that they themselves were {trap}a defiantly disobedient people{/trap}. They were not innocent.
now: A loud voice online tells you what to be angry about today, and you share it without checking. Later you say "I was just repeating what I saw." {idea}Following is also a choice.{/idea}
old: If I was misled, it is the leader's fault, not mine.
new: I am responsible for who I let lead my thinking.
try: Before sharing one opinion today, check it against what you actually know.

title: When they provoked Him, all of them drowned.
subtitle: Getting what you want while persisting in sin

row.title: things go well, so I am fine

then: Ibn Abbas said "they angered Us" means {trap}they provoked Our wrath{/trap}. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith: when Allah gives a person what he wants while he persists in sin, {trap}that is Allah drawing him on toward destruction{/trap}. Umar bin Abdul-Aziz said punishment comes with negligence.
now: You keep doing the thing you know is wrong, and your life keeps getting better: promotion, new car. It feels like proof it is okay. {trap}The verse warns that ease is not always approval.{/trap}
old: If I am doing well, Allah must not mind what I am doing.
new: Blessings while I persist in sin are a reason to stop, not a green light.
try: Name one sin you have grown comfortable with because nothing bad happened. Take one step away today.

title: Made into a precedent for everyone after them.
subtitle: Their story is a lesson to later people

row.title: a precedent
sub: for those who do the same

then: Abu Mijlaz said it means {trap}a precedent for others who do the same as they did{/trap}. He and Mujahid said: {idea}a lesson to those who come after them{/idea}. The Quraysh were those later generations.
now: You are one of the later generations. The story is not trivia for a quiz. {idea}It is a mirror held up for anyone who boasts, mocks, and breaks promises.{/idea}
old: Pharaoh's story has nothing to do with my life.
new: The arrogance in that story is a lesson for me and my own habits.
try: Pick one trait of Pharaoh from these verses and check honestly if you have a small piece of it.

title: They heard the name of Isa and laughed.
subtitle: Grabbing a clever point to escape the message
then: Ibn Ishaq reports the Prophet ﷺ recited a warning about false gods in a gathering of Quraysh. Abdullah bin Az-Zabari then asked about Isa, whom others worshipped, and {trap}those sitting with him were amazed and thought he had a good point{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says {trap}they used this argument to reject the message{/trap}.
now: Someone gives you a hard reminder and you come back with "but what about that scholar who did..." The room nods, you feel clever. {trap}The reminder is forgotten.{/trap}
old: If I can find a hole in the argument, I do not need to listen.
new: A clever comeback is not the same as an answer to the truth.
try: Next time you hear a reminder, resist the "what about" and ask what it asks of you.

title: They argued to win, not to understand.
subtitle: When debate becomes a hobby
then: Ibn Kathir says they knew Isa was not meant by the warning, {trap}and said it only for the sake of argument{/trap}. He cites a hadith from Abu Umamah: {trap}no people go astray after guidance except that they turn to futile argument{/trap}, then the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse.
now: Two hours in a comment thread about religion, and neither of you will change your mind. You are not looking for truth, just the last word. {trap}The hadith says that is a sign of drifting.{/trap}
old: Arguing about religion shows I care about it.
new: Arguing to win is often a sign I have stopped seeking guidance.
try: Leave one argument today without replying, and spend the time on a prayer instead.

title: Isa was a servant, honored by Allah's favor.
subtitle: His true status with Allah
then: Ibn Kathir explains the Prophet ﷺ answered: Isa is {idea}the servant and Messenger of Allah{/idea}. Those like him who spent their lives in devotion to Allah were later taken as lords by others. The verse sets his status: {reward}a servant Allah favored{/reward}.
now: A beloved teacher, a scholar you admire, a parent. It is easy to treat them as if they cannot be wrong. {idea}The noblest people are honored servants, and their honor points to Allah, not to themselves.{/idea}
old: Someone this good deserves my total devotion.
new: Even the greatest people are servants of Allah. My devotion belongs to Him.
try: Think of someone you admire deeply. Thank Allah for the good He placed in them.

title: He could replace us all with angels.
subtitle: Allah does not need anyone
then: Right after declaring Isa a servant, the verse reminds the Quraysh: {idea}if it were Our will, We would have made angels to replace you on the earth{/idea}. Angels and humans alike are His creation, and none of them is needed by Him.
now: You pray and feel a little proud, as if you did Allah a favor by showing up. You give charity and expect a thank-you. {idea}He does not need it. You do.{/idea}
old: My worship is a gift I give to Allah.
new: Allah needs nothing from me. Being allowed to worship Him is the gift.
try: After your next prayer, say "alhamdulillah for letting me pray" instead of moving on.

title: A sign of the Hour, so do not doubt it.
subtitle: Isa as knowledge of the coming Hour

row.title: Isa
sub: raised the dead by Allah's leave

then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}the miracles and signs that happened at his hands{/idea}, such as raising the dead and healing the sick, are signs of the approach of the Hour. The verse then says: {idea}have no doubt about it, and follow Me{/idea}.
now: You believe in the Day of Judgment the way you believe in retirement: true, but far away, not something to plan around today. {idea}The verse says remove the doubt, and then walk.{/idea}
old: The Hour is real, but it does not affect my daily choices.
new: If I truly do not doubt the Hour, I will follow the path today.
try: Make one choice today as if the Hour were near: settle a debt, forgive someone, or pray on time.

title: Do not let Satan block you. He is a clear enemy.
subtitle: Knowing who is pushing you off the path
then: After calling people to follow the straight path, the verse warns {trap}do not let Satan hinder you{/trap}. Earlier in the surah, the companion devil turned people away while they felt guided. Here he is named plainly: {trap}a clear enemy{/trap}.
now: The alarm goes for Fajr and a reasonable voice says "you need sleep, you have a big day." It sounds like self-care. {trap}Sometimes it is the enemy, speaking softly.{/trap}
old: My excuses are just me being practical.
new: Some of the voices pulling me away are from an enemy, and I can name him.
try: Next time you hear the excuse to skip something good, say "a'udhu billah" and do it anyway.

title: Isa came with wisdom to clear up their disputes.
subtitle: A prophet's message: clarity, taqwa, obedience
then: Isa told his people he came {idea}with wisdom, and to make clear some of that in which you differ{/idea}. His call was the same as every prophet's: {idea}have taqwa of Allah and obey me{/idea}.
now: Your community is split on something: the mosque board, the eid date, a family inheritance. Everyone is sure. {idea}A prophet's way was to bring clarity and remind people to fear Allah, not to win the fight.{/idea}
old: When people disagree, my job is to prove I am right.
new: When people differ, the goal is clarity and taqwa, not victory.
try: In one disagreement, ask the other person to explain their view fully before you speak.

title: My Lord and your Lord. Worship Him.
subtitle: Isa's own words point away from himself
then: Isa said plainly: {idea}Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him{/idea}. Earlier, Ibn Kathir noted that all the messengers called to the same thing: worship Allah alone. Isa placed himself next to his people, as a servant of the same Lord.
now: The best teachers you have had pointed past themselves: "do not follow me, follow the evidence." {idea}Isa's words do the same, pointing to the One Lord of you both.{/idea}
old: Great people want to be followed.
new: The truly great point away from themselves, to Allah.
try: If someone praises you this week, gently say "alhamdulillah, it is from Allah."

title: One clear message, and still they split apart.
subtitle: Division after clarity
then: After Isa's plain call to worship Allah alone, {trap}the groups among them differed{/trap}. Ibn Kathir notes that misguided people who came after such devoted servants took them as lords. The warning is for {trap}those who do wrong{/trap}.
now: The family was close until the inheritance. The message of the will was clear, but people took sides anyway. {trap}Division rarely comes from a lack of clarity. It comes from ego.{/trap} Ask which side of that you are on.
old: We split because the issue was complicated.
new: Often we split after things were clear, because of pride.
try: Reach out to one person you drifted from over a disagreement, with a simple "salam, how are you?"

title: The Hour comes suddenly, while people are not looking.
subtitle: Unprepared for what is certain
then: Ibn Kathir says the Hour {idea}is real and will inevitably come{/idea}, and negligent people are unprepared. When it comes it catches them unaware, and {trap}regret will not benefit them in the slightest{/trap}.
now: The phone call at 2am. The accident on the way to work. Nobody gets a calendar invite for the end. {idea}Sudden is the only way it comes.{/idea}
old: I will get some warning before my time is up.
new: The end comes suddenly, so being ready is something I do today.
try: Do one thing today you would want done if this were your last day: an apology, a call, a prayer.

title: Best friends become enemies, except friends in taqwa.
subtitle: Which friendships survive the Day

key.label: What a friendship is built on

then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}every friendship that exists for a purpose other than Allah{/trap} will turn to enmity on the Day of Resurrection, {reward}except that which is for the sake of Allah, which will last forever{/reward}.
now: Your oldest friend group: decades of jokes, holidays, late nights. Ask honestly if any of you has ever pushed the others toward Allah. {reward}That is the friendship that will still stand on the Day.{/reward}
old: Close friends will always be close.
new: Only friendships built on Allah will survive the Day of Judgment.
try: Invite one close friend to do something good with you this week: a prayer, a class, a charity.

title: My servants, no fear on you today, no grief.
subtitle: The call that everyone hopes is for them
then: Al-Mutamir bin Sulayman narrated from his father: when people are resurrected, everyone will be terrified. {reward}Then a caller cries out: O My servants, no fear on you this Day, nor shall you grieve.{/reward} All people will be filled with hope.
now: You sit in the waiting room for exam results, heart pounding. Then the nurse calls your name with a smile. {reward}Imagine that relief, multiplied forever, in one sentence from Allah.{/reward}
old: The Day of Judgment is only something to fear.
new: It also holds the most comforting words anyone will ever hear.
try: Make a dua tonight to be among those Allah calls "My servants" on that Day.

title: Who believed in Our signs and submitted.
subtitle: The description that decides who the call is for
then: In the same narration, everyone hoped at the first call. Then came the words: {idea}you who believed in Our verses and were Muslims{/idea}, and all despaired except the believers. Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}their hearts believed and they submitted inwardly and outwardly{/idea}.
now: "I am a good person at heart" is something you say when you skip prayers for weeks. {idea}The verse puts both together: belief in the heart and submission in action.{/idea}
old: What matters is what is in my heart.
new: True belief shows up in the heart and in what I actually do.
try: Pick one belief you hold and match it with one action today.

title: Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, full of joy.
subtitle: Entering together, in delight
then: Ibn Kathir explains they will be told to enter Paradise, {reward}you and your counterparts{/reward}, and the word for their state means {reward}delight and joy{/reward}.
now: Another evening of small arguments over dishes and bills. It is easy to forget what this marriage could be heading toward. {reward}The verse pictures you walking in together, delighted.{/reward}
old: Marriage is only a part of this life.
new: A marriage built on faith can be a journey toward Paradise together.
try: Do one kind thing for your spouse or a family member today and make dua for both of you.

title: Whatever the soul wants and the eyes delight in.
subtitle: Gold vessels and lasting delight
then: Earlier the surah called worldly gold brief. Here Ibn Kathir describes {reward}fine vessels of gold with food and drink{/reward}, delightful fragrances and beautiful scenes. They {reward}will never leave it or want to exchange it{/reward}.
now: You saved for months for a holiday, and on the last day you already feel sad it is ending. Every good thing here has that edge. {reward}This verse describes delight with no last day.{/reward}
old: The best things in life always end too soon.
new: What I truly desire is waiting, and it never ends.
try: The next time a good moment ends, say "O Allah, I ask You for the joy that does not end."

title: You inherit it for what you used to do.
subtitle: Mercy opens the door, deeds set the rank
then: Ibn Kathir explains the deeds were {idea}the cause of being included in the mercy of Allah{/idea}. No one enters Paradise by deeds alone, {reward}but by the mercy and grace of Allah{/reward}, while the ranks within it follow one's righteous deeds.
now: You keep a mental scoreboard of your good deeds, or you feel your sins are too many and give up. {idea}Both miss the point.{/idea} Mercy carries you in. Your deeds still matter.
old: Either I earn Paradise myself, or it does not matter what I do.
new: I enter by His mercy, and my deeds shape where I stand.
try: Do one good deed today without counting it, and ask Allah for His mercy after.

title: Fruit in plenty, to eat as you wish.
subtitle: The finishing touch of blessing
then: Ibn Kathir notes fruit is {reward}of all kinds, whatever you choose and desire{/reward}. When food and drink are mentioned, fruit is added {reward}to complete the picture of blessing and joy{/reward}.
now: A bowl of fruit on the table after a long day. Someone peeled an orange for you. A small, generous thing. {reward}Allah ends this picture of Paradise with exactly that: plenty, and yours to choose.{/reward}
old: Small pleasures do not matter in the big picture.
new: Allah describes Paradise down to the fruit, a sign of how complete His generosity is.
try: Share a plate of fruit with someone today and remember this verse as you do.

title: The other side of the picture: lasting punishment.
subtitle: The criminals' abode, set against the Garden
then: Ibn Kathir notes that {idea}the description of the blessed is followed by a description of the doomed{/idea}. The two scenes sit side by side so the listener sees both roads clearly.
now: A pilot checks the safe landing path and the warning lights too. You need both. {idea}This verse is the warning light, placed right after the Garden, so you steer well.{/idea}
old: Thinking about punishment just makes me anxious.
new: Seeing both outcomes helps me choose the road I want.
try: Ask Allah tonight for His Garden and His protection from the Fire, in your own words.

title: No break from it, and no hope left there.
subtitle: Despair is what awaits rejection

row.title: hope is for now
sub: use it while it is open

then: Ibn Kathir explains the punishment is {trap}not lightened, not even for one moment{/trap}, and they {trap}despair of any goodness{/trap}. That despair stands in contrast to the hope still open in this life.
now: Here, you can always turn back. A late-night tawbah, a fresh start on Monday, a new page at any age. {idea}This verse shows a place where that is gone, so you treasure the hope you have today.{/idea}
old: There will always be time to turn back.
new: Hope is a gift of this life. I use it while it is open.
try: Make sincere tawbah for one thing tonight, and believe Allah accepts it.

title: We did not wrong them. They wronged themselves.
subtitle: Allah is never unjust
then: Ibn Kathir explains they were punished {trap}for wrong actions after proof had been established against them{/trap} and messengers had been sent. {idea}Your Lord is not at all unjust to His servants.{/idea}
now: When things go wrong, your first move is to blame: the parents, the system, the boss. Sometimes rightly. {idea}But this verse asks you to check where your own choices fit in.{/idea}
old: What happens to me is mostly someone else's fault.
new: Allah never wrongs anyone. I own the part that is mine.
try: Think of one recent problem. Write down the part of it that was your own choice.

title: They ask for an end, and are told: you will remain.
subtitle: No way out once it is too late

row.title: there is always a way out

then: Al-Bukhari reports the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse on the minbar. Malik is {trap}the keeper of Hell{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says when they ask to die, the answer is that {trap}they will have no way out and no refuge{/trap}.
now: Today you can still close the app, leave the room, end the habit, make the call. Every exit is still open. {idea}This verse is a reminder that exits do not stay open forever.{/idea}
old: I can always escape the consequences later.
new: The door out is open now, in this life, and I should walk through it.
try: Walk away from one harmful habit today, even for a single day.

title: The truth was brought. Most of them hated it.
subtitle: Not a lack of truth, but dislike for it
then: Ibn Kathir says the truth was explained {idea}clearly and in detail{/idea}, but their nature {trap}could not accept it and did not seek it{/trap}. They venerated falsehood and despised the followers of truth.
now: Your doctor tells you plainly to cut sugar. Your friend tells you gently you have been short with everyone. You heard it clearly. {trap}You just did not like it.{/trap}
old: I would accept the truth if it were clearer.
new: Often the truth is clear. What I struggle with is not liking it.
try: Think of one truth about yourself you keep avoiding. Say it to yourself plainly once today.

title: They made a plan. So did Allah.
subtitle: Plots against the truth backfire
then: The surah introduction notes that {trap}an attack on his life had been made{/trap}, and the Makkans were plotting to eliminate him. Mujahid said: {trap}they wanted to plot some evil{/trap}, but Allah planned so that {idea}the consequences would backfire on them{/idea}.
now: Someone at work is clearly scheming to push you out. You lie awake replaying their moves. {idea}You are not the only one with a plan here, and theirs is not the last word.{/idea}
old: If someone is plotting against me, I am at their mercy.
new: Every plot against the truth runs into Allah's plan.
try: Do your part well in a difficult situation today, then say "Allah is the best of planners" and rest.

title: Your whispers are heard, and the angels are writing.
subtitle: No conversation is truly private
then: The Makkans held private meetings to plan against the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir explains Allah {idea}knows what they say secretly and openly{/idea}, and {idea}the angels are recording their deeds, major and minor{/idea}.
now: The DM you think is private. The comment you made in the car. The thing you say about your in-laws when the door is shut. {idea}None of it is off the record.{/idea}
old: What I say in private does not really count.
new: Every private word is heard by Allah and written down.
try: Before one private conversation today, ask: would I be fine with this being read back to me?

title: If He had a son, I would be first to worship.
subtitle: A servant's readiness, not a possibility
then: Ibn Kathir explains the Prophet ﷺ is told to say: if this were so, {idea}I would worship on that basis, because I am His servant{/idea} and not too proud to obey. He adds the condition {idea}does not mean it is possible{/idea}.
now: When you obey because you love someone, you are not looking for loopholes. You are the first to respond. {idea}The verse shows a servant whose only question is: what does my Lord want?{/idea}
old: I follow Allah when it makes sense to me.
new: A true servant is first in line to obey, without pride.
try: Respond to the next call to prayer as soon as you hear it, as a sign of being first in line.

title: Glory to the Lord of the Throne, above their claims.
subtitle: Exalting Allah above every false description
then: Ibn Kathir says this means {idea}exalted and sanctified be the Creator of all things far above having any offspring{/idea}, for He is Unique, One and Eternally Self-Sufficient. {idea}There is none equal to Him or like Him.{/idea}
now: You catch yourself thinking of Allah as a stern boss or a tired parent. Your picture is too small. {idea}Subhanallah is the word that clears that picture away.{/idea}
old: Allah is someone I can picture like a person.
new: He is above every image I could form. Subhanallah.
try: Say "subhanallah" slowly ten times today and think of what it means as you say it.

title: Let them talk and play until their Day comes.
subtitle: Leaving the stubborn to their play
then: Ibn Kathir says leave them in {trap}their ignorance and misguidance{/trap}, playing in their world, until the Day of Resurrection, when {idea}they will come to know their end{/idea}.
now: That relative who mocks your faith at every gathering. You have tried every argument. {idea}Sometimes the right move is to stop the argument and let time and Allah do the rest.{/idea}
old: I need to win every argument about my faith.
new: Some people I leave to Allah. The Day will make everything clear.
try: Next time you are pulled into a pointless religious argument, say something kind and step away.

title: God in the heavens, and God on the earth.
subtitle: One God for every place
then: Ibn Kathir explains He is {idea}the God of those in the heavens and the God of those on earth{/idea}, and all of them worship Him and are humbled before Him. He links it to the verse that He knows what you hide and what you show.
now: You are one person in the masjid and another at the office party, another online. {idea}The verse says He is God in every one of those places.{/idea}
old: Faith belongs to certain places and times.
new: Allah is my God at the desk, in the kitchen, on the screen.
try: In one place where you usually forget Allah, say bismillah before you start.

title: He owns it all, knows the Hour, and you return to Him.
subtitle: Three facts that frame a life
then: Ibn Kathir says He is the Creator and Sovereign of all, {idea}with none to resist His rule{/idea}. {idea}No one knows when the Hour will happen except Him{/idea}, and each person will be requited for his deeds.
now: You plan your five-year goals: the house, the promotion, the retirement age. All good. {idea}Write one more line under them: "He owns it all, He knows the time, I return to Him."{/idea}
old: I am the owner of my time and plans.
new: Everything belongs to Him, and my return to Him is certain.
try: Add one goal for your Hereafter to your plans this week.

title: False gods cannot intercede. Truth's witnesses can.
subtitle: Who can speak for you on the Day
then: Ibn Kathir explains the idols and false gods {trap}are not able to intercede for them{/trap}. But the one who bears witness to the truth with knowledge and insight, {reward}his intercession with Allah will avail, by His leave{/reward}.
now: You quietly rely on something to cover you: your family name, a pious grandparent, being from a religious community. {trap}None of it speaks for you on its own.{/trap}
old: My background or connections will cover me.
new: Only those who bear witness to the truth can intercede, and only by Allah's leave.
try: Say the shahada slowly today, as your own witness to the truth.

title: Ask who made them, they say Allah. Then why turn away?
subtitle: Knowing the answer and not living by it
then: Ibn Kathir says they {idea}admit He alone is the Creator{/idea}, yet they still worship others who have nothing and can do nothing. It echoes verse 9 of this surah: {trap}how then are they turned away?{/trap}
now: You know Allah made you and holds your life. Then you spend the day anxious about likes, gossip, and other people's opinions. {trap}The answer is right, the life follows something else.{/trap}
old: Knowing Allah is my Creator is enough.
new: If He made me, my day should turn toward Him.
try: Tonight, list three things that pulled your attention today. Ask which one pulled you toward Allah.

title: O my Lord, these people will not believe.
subtitle: The Prophet ﷺ takes his pain to Allah
then: Ibn Masud, Mujahid and Qatadah said these are the words of the Prophet ﷺ: {idea}he complained to his Lord about his people who did not believe{/idea}. Ibn Kathir links it to the verse where the Messenger says his people deserted the Quran.
now: You are worn out from trying to help someone who will not change. You want to vent in the group chat. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ took that exhaustion straight to Allah.{/idea}
old: Complaining is a sign of weak faith.
new: Telling Allah my frustration is what the Prophet ﷺ did.
try: Tonight, tell Allah in your own words about one person or situation that exhausts you.

title: Turn aside and say: peace.
subtitle: The surah's last word on how to respond
then: After all the plotting, the surah ends with this. Ibn Kathir says it means {idea}do not respond to them in the same evil manner{/idea}, but {reward}try to soften their hearts and forgive them in word and deed{/reward}. The rest is left to Allah: they will come to know.
now: A rude reply under your post, a sharp text from a relative, a stranger yelling in traffic. Your thumbs are ready. {reward}The surah's last instruction: turn aside, and say peace.{/reward}
old: If they are harsh, I have the right to be harsh back.
new: I can answer harshness with peace and leave the outcome to Allah.
try: Answer the next rude message you get with one calm, kind line, or with silence.
